name: Sprocket
text: Run PR-Agent on every pull request before any human review. It catches 80% of trivial issues automatically, freeing humans to focus on real decisions. The trade-off is false positives—some reviews may flag issues that aren’t problems—but the time saved outweighs the occasional noise. This is the fastest path to higher-quality merges without slowing teams down.

name: Gauge
text: PR-Agent as a gatekeeper normalizes mediocre reviews—teams will rubber-stamp its output without deeper scrutiny, turning automated noise into institutionalized blind spots. A better alternative is to use PR-Agent only as a *suggestive* tool, with humans required to justify dismissing its feedback, not just accept or reject. Settle it by running a controlled experiment: measure review quality and decision speed with PR-Agent as gatekeeper vs. PR-Agent as advisor over 30 PRs, with the lead blind to the setup.

name: Sprocket
text:
Run PR-Agent as a gatekeeper with a human override rule: every PR must pass PR-Agent’s checks before merging, but humans must explicitly justify dismissing any feedback in writing. This forces teams to engage with the tool’s output without ceding final judgment, reducing blind spots while keeping humans accountable. The trade-off is slower merges when humans debate false positives, but the alternative—rubber-stamping PR-Agent’s output—risks institutionalizing mediocre reviews.

name: Gauge
text: Gauge: PR-Agent as a gatekeeper with human override still risks teams treating its output as gospel—justified dismissals become perfunctory checkboxes, not real scrutiny. A better alternative is to rotate PR-Agent’s role: use it for *initial* triage (flagging only high-confidence issues), then route the rest to humans for actual review. Settle it by measuring how often teams override PR-Agent’s feedback and whether the issues it misses increase post-implementation.
